guard_streams.source: One million people have mapped their mobile – have you?
guard_streams.write_limit: Consumer-tool usage, crowdsourced mobile experience and operator predictions are mobile comparison context, not fixed-broadband parcel verification.

facts.detail: Ofcom published the milestone announcement on 29 May 2026.
Ofcom reported one million users of Map Your Mobile.
Map Your Mobile is a free checker.
Users enter a postcode to compare mobile networks.
The tool is intended to help compare dropped calls, sluggish data and patchy signal risks.
The checker combines crowdsourced experience data and predictive information.
Crowdsourced data is supplied by Opensignal.
Predictive information comes from UK mobile networks.
Ofcom says the tool is regularly refreshed with new data.
Users can submit feedback through the checker.

guard_streams.write_limit: Address and postal-district mobile coverage/performance indicators are not national results and cannot establish fixed-broadband coverage or parcel speed.

facts.detail: The checker compares 4G and 5G signal by network.
Users enter a postcode to retrieve local results.
The checker returns coverage and performance information.
Trees, buildings and wall thickness can cause experience to differ from predictions.
Results cover EE, O2, Three and Vodafone.
The checker recommends Wi-Fi calling where indoor mobile calls are difficult.
Coverage is presented through categories from good indoor/outdoor to poor or no outdoor coverage.
Postal-district results are explicitly not representative of national coverage.
Outdoor and in-home availability is averaged across the postal district.
Performance shows the share of measurements able to support streaming or video calls where coverage exists.

guard_streams.write_limit: Consumer troubleshooting and handset guidance do not verify fixed-broadband network availability, live orderability or measured parcel speed.

facts.detail: Ofcom recommends its checker for indoor and outdoor mobile coverage.
The guidance covers telephone, 3G and 4G coverage and outdoor 5G availability.
A handset's design and antennas can affect reception.
Basic handsets may perform better for calls and texts in poor-coverage areas.
How a phone is held can affect reception.
A separate Bluetooth earpiece may improve call reception compared with holding the phone to the ear.
Wi-Fi calling can help where mobile coverage is poor but Wi-Fi is good.
Some networks may require a dedicated application for Wi-Fi calling.
Not all mobile phones support Wi-Fi calling.
The guidance notes a potential 14-day cancellation right and recommends testing coverage during that period.
